story:
🍓 The Receipt in the Melon Crate

Star Strawberry had always been the one people watched, and that Saturday the farmers market watched her walk past the melon crates with her chin up and her hands 🤚 shaking. She had rehearsed the lie for eleven days. Peter Banana waited by the honey stall 🍯 holding two coffees like a man who still believed in his own marriage. He kissed her cheek. He asked about her morning. He did not mention the receipt 🧾 folded in his back pocket.

Enzo Eggplant arrived at ten, the way he always did, in sunglasses 🕶 he did not need and a linen shirt he could not afford. Star felt the old heat rise in her throat. Three weeks of stolen afternoons, and every one of them had felt like weather 🌦 — something that happened to her rather than something she chose. Across the aisle, Bianca Broccoli was buying plums 🟣 she had no intention of eating, and watching.

The confrontation came fast and quiet. Peter set the coffees down, unfolded the receipt, and read the address of the motel out loud in the voice he used for grocery lists 💔. Star did not deny it. What she said instead was worse. "How long have you known?" And Peter, who had never once surprised her in eleven years, said, "Since the first afternoon."

Because Peter had not discovered anything. Peter had been told. Bianca Broccoli had walked into his office in the spring with a folder 📁 and a proposal, and Peter Banana, who could never say no to anyone and least of all to his mother-in-law, had agreed to wait, and to watch, and to let his wife ruin herself in public where the family lawyer could see it.

That was the first thing Star had not known. The second arrived eleven seconds later, when Enzo Eggplant crossed the aisle, set an envelope 📩 on the melon crate, and said he was finished. Bianca had hired him in February. Six payments, one seduction, one witness statement, and the Broccoli estate would pass cleanly to the grandchildren with Star cut out of it entirely. Enzo had taken five payments. He had refused the sixth, because somewhere in the third week he had stopped performing 🖤, and that ruined everything for Bianca, who needed a liar, and for Star, who had been counting on one.

Bianca's plums hit the pavement. She reached for the envelope and Enzo slid it out of her reach ✋ with the same lazy grace he used for everything. Inside, he said, were forty minutes of recordings 🎧 — her instructions, her prices, her exact words about her own daughter.

And Star Strawberry laughed 😶‍🌫️, not the laugh of a woman caught but the laugh of a woman watching a long plan finally land.

Because she had known about February since February. Enzo had told her the night he refused the money, and together they had decided to let Bianca keep building 🧩 the trap, all the way to the melon crates, in front of the whole market, where it could never be taken back. The affair had been real. The recordings had always been hers.

What none of them had planned for was Peter, who picked up the envelope nobody was guarding, opened it, and went very still ❄ — because the recordings were not the only thing inside. There was a single sheet of paper, dated four years ago, with a clinic letterhead 📄 and two names on it, and neither of those names was Enzo's. "Star," he said, and his voice had nothing left in it at all. "Whose is this?"

premise: my roommate ate my leftovers and lied about it
story:
🥑 Whoever Ate The Tupperware Knows What They Did

Cass Cucumber had labelled the container. That was the part Avi Avocado kept coming back to 🧊 — the little strip of masking tape, the careful block capitals, the date. You do not label a thing unless you expect somebody to take it.

For eleven days the apartment ran on a thin, polite silence. Cass asked twice. Avi said no twice, and each time his pit 🪨 sat a little heavier in him, because the truth was he had eaten it, standing at the counter at one in the morning, joylessly, the way you eat something that is not yours.

Those eleven days had a texture. Avi started buying his own milk and labelling it back, which felt like a declaration of war conducted entirely through masking tape 📏. Cass began washing dishes at odd hours. They passed each other in the hallway with the elaborate courtesy of people who have decided the other one is a liar, and the fridge hummed between them like a witness being kept off the stand.

Twice Avi nearly confessed. Both times Cass said something so precisely wounded 😔 — about trust, about how she would never, about how it was not even the food, it was the principle — that confessing would have been the same as handing her a weapon. So he said nothing, and the not-saying hardened in him, and by day nine he had begun to resent a woman he had genuinely wronged.

On the twelfth day Cass produced the photograph. Not of Avi. Of the fridge 🧊 at 1:04am, timestamped, sent to her by the building's smart camera, and in it you could see quite clearly that the container was already gone.

Avi looked at it for a long moment. "That's an hour before I got up," he said, and watched Cass's grip 🤚 tighten on her phone, and understood that she already knew.

Because Cass had eaten it. Cass had eaten it on day one, cried about it, labelled a second container with the same tape and the same date, and staged eleven days of wounded questions so that nobody would look at the thing she actually needed hidden — which was not lunch.

It was the lease. Her name had come off it in March 📄, quietly, at her mother's insistence, and Bianca Broccoli had put her own on instead, and the rent Avi had been handing over every month had been going somewhere it had no business going.

"You let me apologise," Avi said slowly, "for eleven days," and Cass's skin 💧 went waxy and pale.

What neither of them had allowed for was Bianca, who had been listening from the hallway 👀 with her coat still on, and who now stepped into the kitchen holding a second photograph. Same camera. Same night. 1:04am.

In it, the person taking the container out of the fridge was not Cass, and it was not Avi, and the coat they were wearing 🧥 was the one Bianca had on right now.

"Sit down, both of you," Bianca said gently, pulling out a chair 🪑. "There's something about the lease I should have told you in March."

Avi did not sit. He was looking past her, at the hallway, at the front door standing open on the dark, and at the third pair of shoes 👞 just inside it — shoes he had not seen in four years, and had buried a man in.

"Whose are those?"

🍋 The Sourest Woman At The Funeral

Lorna Lemon wore grey to bury her husband and everyone agreed she wore it beautifully ⚱. She stood at the front of the orchard chapel with her rind still tight and green at the stem, accepting condolences like a woman receiving invoices.

Nobody mentioned the smell of smoke. Nobody mentioned that Vito Olive had been the one to find the body, or that he had found it very early 🕛, or that he had arrived at the chapel in a suit two sizes too generous for him.

"He was a good man," said Vito, pressing Lorna's hand 🤝 a fraction longer than was decent.

"He was not," said Lorna, "but thank you."

What the mourners did notice was how well Lorna managed the room. She remembered every name. She asked after a cousin's surgery, complimented a hat 👒, steered two feuding brothers to opposite pews, and did it all with the terrible competence of a woman who has rehearsed a day for months. Grief makes people clumsy. Lorna had never been clumsier than a blade.

Her husband had been sweet, and stupid, and eleven years younger than the marriage certificate claimed, and he had spent the last of the grove money on a boat ⛵ nobody had ever seen in water. When they found him in the pressing room the coroner used the word "accident" and Lorna had nodded as though accepting a gift.

The will was read in the vestry at four. Everything to Lorna, which surprised nobody, and the pickling plant to Vito, which surprised everyone including Vito, whose glass 🍷 stopped halfway to his mouth. Lorna did not look up. She had signed that clause herself in February, forging a hand she had spent thirty years learning, and she had signed it because a man who inherits a business is a man with a motive.

That was her first mistake, and it was beautiful 📄, and it held for exactly nine minutes.

At four past four the notary cleared his throat and produced a second envelope, dated later, witnessed properly, and in it her husband had left everything — the house, the groves, the name — to a woman in another town, and the woman's name was Lorna Lemon.

Not her. Another one. The first one 💍. The one he had never divorced, whose existence made thirty years of Lorna's marriage a legal fiction and her signature on the February clause a felony committed on behalf of a stranger.

Lorna's juice 💧 went to acid in her. She looked at the notary, and then at Vito, and Vito was already smiling, because Vito had known since December and had let her build the whole thing.

And at the back of the chapel, quietly, a door opened 🚪.

The woman who came in was small and sharp and unmistakably lemon, and she walked up the aisle 👜 past every relative Lorna had ever lied to, and stopped at the coffin, and did not look inside it.

"Open it," she said. "He isn't in there."

Lorna turned, very slowly, toward a coffin she had personally chosen, sealed, and never once asked to see.

"Why would you say that?"
